topic.title: Why Your Pupils Are Different Sizes
topic.audience_question: Why can one pupil look larger than the other, and which patterns need emergency assessment?
topic.pubmed_query: anisocoria physiologic pharmacologic third nerve palsy Horner syndrome emergency evaluation

sources.title: What Is Anisocoria?
sources.abstract: The American Academy of Ophthalmology explains that anisocoria means unequal pupil size. It can be a normal variation, but a new difference may reflect eye disease, nerve dysfunction, medicine exposure, injury, or another serious condition requiring assessment.

sources.title: Anisocoria
sources.abstract: This current American Academy of Ophthalmology EyeWiki review describes physiologic anisocoria as the most common form, affecting up to 20 percent of people and usually producing a small, stable difference. It outlines evaluation in bright and dim light and important ocular, neurological, traumatic, and pharmacological causes.

sources.title: Anisocoria
sources.abstract: MedlinePlus notes that slight pupil-size differences occur in many healthy people. A sudden or persistent new difference, especially after injury or with blurred or double vision, drooping eyelid, headache, eye pain, nausea, vomiting, or vision loss, requires medical assessment.

sources.title: Horner Syndrome
sources.abstract: The American Academy of Ophthalmology EyeWiki review describes Horner syndrome as impaired sympathetic nerve supply causing a smaller pupil and subtle eyelid droop, sometimes with reduced facial sweating. Acute painful Horner syndrome is a neurological emergency because carotid artery dissection must be considered.

sources.title: Acquired Oculomotor Nerve Palsy
sources.abstract: This current EyeWiki review explains that third-nerve palsy may cause eyelid droop, abnormal eye movement, double vision, and an enlarged pupil. An acute complete pupil-involving palsy is an emergency in which an intracranial aneurysm must be urgently excluded.

sources.title: Incidence and Etiologies of Acquired Third Nerve Palsy Using a Population-Based Method
sources.abstract: This population-based study found several causes of acquired third-nerve palsy, including microvascular disease, trauma, tumors, surgery, and aneurysmal compression. Pupil involvement was more frequent with compressive lesions, but pupil findings alone did not reliably exclude a compressive cause.

sources.title: Anisocoria
sources.abstract: This clinical review covers physiologic anisocoria, tonic pupil, medication exposure, iris injury, third-nerve palsy, and Horner syndrome. It recommends urgent imaging when acute anisocoria suggests a compressive third-nerve palsy or acute Horner syndrome.

episode.title: E45: Why Your Pupils Are Different Sizes
episode.hook: Hello and welcome to the Your Only Doc podcast. Imagine opening the front camera and noticing that one black circle in your eyes looks larger than the other. You check another photograph, turn toward a lamp, and worry that something has suddenly changed. Unequal pupils are called anisocoria. Sometimes the difference is a harmless lifelong variation. Sometimes it is the first visible clue to a problem in the eye, a nerve, or a blood vessel.

sections.heading: The high yield summary
sections.narration: Too busy? Here is your high yield summary. A small, stable pupil difference without symptoms is common and may be normal. What matters is whether it is new, which pupil behaves abnormally in light or darkness, and what comes with it. Seek emergency care for sudden unequal pupils after head or eye injury, or with severe headache, neck pain, eye pain, drooping eyelid, double vision, weakness, speech difficulty, confusion, vomiting, or vision loss. Do not diagnose the cause from a photograph alone.
on_screen: A small stable difference may be normal
Sudden neurological signs need emergency care

sections.heading: Pupils should change with the light
sections.narration: The pupil is an opening controlled by muscles in the iris. It becomes smaller in bright light and larger in darkness. Parasympathetic nerves constrict it, while sympathetic nerves help it dilate. The two pupils are not required to match to the fraction of a millimeter at every moment. The clinical question is whether one pupil fails to constrict, fails to dilate, has an irregular shape, or is accompanied by an abnormal eyelid or eye movement.

sections.heading: A harmless difference is surprisingly common
sections.narration: Physiologic anisocoria is the most common explanation. It can affect up to one in five people and usually creates a small difference, often no more than about one millimeter. Vision, eyelid position, and eye movements remain normal. Old photographs may show that it has been present for years. Even so, a person cannot safely label a newly noticed difference as physiologic until concerning symptoms, medication exposure, trauma, and eye or nerve disease have been considered.
on_screen: Up to one in five people

sections.heading: Light and darkness help locate the problem
sections.narration: Clinicians compare both pupils in bright and dim conditions. If the difference becomes greater in bright light, the larger pupil may not be constricting normally. If it becomes greater in darkness, the smaller pupil may not be dilating normally. This framework narrows the possibilities, but phone flashes, camera exposure, viewing angle, and room lighting can create misleading photographs. Use images only to show timing or change, not to perform a home neurological examination.

sections.heading: Medicines can reach one eye
sections.narration: Eye drops used during an examination are an obvious cause, but accidental exposure also matters. Scopolamine from a motion-sickness patch, certain nebulized or inhaled medicines, plant chemicals, or other anticholinergic products can enlarge one pupil if transferred to one eye. Some glaucoma drops can make one pupil smaller. Wash your hands after handling patches or medicines and tell the clinician about every exposure. Do not place random drops in the eye to test whether the pupil changes.
on_screen: One-eye exposure can change one pupil

sections.heading: A large pupil with droop or double vision is urgent
sections.narration: The third cranial nerve helps lift the eyelid, move the eye, and constrict the pupil. A palsy can produce a drooping eyelid, double vision, an eye that points outward and downward, and sometimes a large poorly reactive pupil. Compression by an aneurysm is one dangerous cause. Pupil size alone cannot prove or exclude it. Sudden onset, especially with headache or eye pain, needs emergency neurological and vascular imaging rather than a routine appointment.
on_screen: Third nerve controls lid, movement, and pupil

sections.heading: A small pupil with droop can indicate Horner syndrome
sections.narration: Horner syndrome interrupts the sympathetic pathway to one side of the face. The affected pupil is smaller and dilates slowly in darkness, while the upper eyelid may droop slightly. Facial sweating can also change. The nerve pathway runs from the brain through the neck and chest, so the cause may lie far from the eye. New Horner syndrome with sudden headache or neck pain is a neurological emergency because injury to the carotid artery must be considered.
on_screen: Small pupil and subtle lid droop
The pathway runs through head, neck, and chest
Painful sudden Horner pattern is an emergency

sections.heading: How clinicians investigate unequal pupils
sections.narration: Now, let us go deeper. The examination measures pupils in light and darkness, tests their reaction to light and near focus, checks eyelids and eye movements, and looks for iris injury or inflammation with a slit lamp. The clinician reviews old photographs, recent trauma, surgery, medicines, headache, neck pain, and neurological symptoms. Selected eye drops may help confirm a pattern, but imaging of the brain, blood vessels, neck, or chest is chosen according to the suspected pathway and urgency.
on_screen: Target imaging to the suspected cause

sections.heading: Three essential takeaways
sections.narration: Number one, a small pupil difference that is longstanding and symptom-free is often physiologic, but a new difference needs an explanation. Number two, review medicines and exposures, compare old photographs, and let a clinician determine which pupil is abnormal instead of self-testing with drops. Number three, seek emergency care when unequal pupils appear suddenly after injury or with severe headache, neck or eye pain, drooping eyelid, double vision, weakness, speech difficulty, confusion, vomiting, or vision loss.

episode.closing: On the next episode, we will explain why one eyelid can start drooping, from fatigue and eyelid changes to muscle, nerve, and brain warning signs. Until then, remember that pupil size matters most when the change is new and another symptom arrives with it.
episode.description: Unequal pupils can be a common normal variation, a medication effect, an eye problem, third-nerve palsy, or Horner syndrome. This episode explains light and dark patterns, associated warning signs, clinical evaluation, and when anisocoria requires emergency care.
